clue.text: From A to E, a cliche to be smashed - kill waffle also

definitions.text: From A to E, a cliche

indicators.note: smashed things lie in broken pieces, so the words that follow must be broken up and reassembled

blocks.note: the fourteen letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A writer vows to smash every stale phrase in the alphabet and cut out all the padding too.
explanation.walkthrough: 'From A to E' describes ALL WALKS OF LIFE itself: the phrase begins with A and ends with E, and it is also a well-worn cliche.
explanation.definitionFit: The stock expression for people of every class and background is a hackneyed phrase whose letters happen to start at A and finish at E.

clue.text: Swirl has rope-maker producing 15s

definitions.note: the clue describes what the answer does; the answer is a noun phrase

indicators.note: a maker turns raw material into something new, so these letters are worked into a fresh order

blocks.note: the twelve letters taken as written

explanation.surface: Twisting fibres together is how a rope-maker produces lengths of cord.
explanation.walkthrough: 15 is MAYFLOWER, so 15s are May flowers: the old rhyme says April showers bring May flowers. 'Rope-maker' looks like one unit, but 'rope' is fodder and 'maker' the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb holds that spring rain in the fourth month brings the blossoms of the following month, so the rain produces the blooms.

clue.text: Put up with your starter being like my sauces!

indicators.note: a starter is what comes first, so only the opening letter of the preceding word is used

blocks.note: to lump it is to put up with something unwelcome
the opening letter of your

explanation.surface: A self-mocking cook warns the diner they will have to tolerate the gravy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lump it' is an informal idiom meaning to accept something you dislike. The setter confesses that his sauces are full of clots.
explanation.definitionFit: Badly made sauces are full of clots, so the setter jokingly describes his own cooking as having that texture.

clue.text: Sequel to a lot of parents accepting time at school

indicators.note: a lot of something is most of it but not all, so the end of the word is dropped
to accept is to take in, so the shortened word takes the other piece inside it

blocks.note: taken as written
fathers are parents
a school year is divided into terms

explanation.surface: Mums and dads take time out to attend school events as a follow-up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a lot of parents' takes one word for a parent in the plural and drops its last two letters; the school period sits after its F.
explanation.definitionFit: Consequences that follow on from an event form its aftermath, the thing that comes after it, much like a follow-up.

clue.text: Brunel's animal, say

blocks.note: first meaning: the middle name of the engineer Isambard ... Brunel
second meaning: one of the great divisions of living things, the animal one being an example

explanation.walkthrough: Isambard Kingdom Brunel was the Victorian engineer of the Great Western Railway; the animal kingdom is a biological category.
explanation.definitionFit: The engineer's middle name is the same word as the biological top-level group that includes animals and plants.

clue.text: River meadow concerned (joining her man) with race relations

definitions.text: concerned (joining her man) with race relations

blocks.note: the Ouse is an English river
a ley is a meadow or grassland

explanation.surface: A riverside field where a woman meets her husband becomes a matter of community relations.
explanation.walkthrough: 'her man' joined up gives Herman: Sir Herman Ouseley chaired Britain's Commission for Racial Equality.
explanation.definitionFit: Herman Ouseley headed the UK Commission for Racial Equality, so his surname belongs to a man concerned with race relations.

clue.text: American city study on which a lot hangs?

definitions.note: the clue describes a thing; the answer is an adjective for it

blocks.note: LA is Los Angeles
a den is a private study

explanation.surface: A Los Angeles study on which much depends.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a crucial piece of research; read literally, something with a lot hanging on it is heavily loaded.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that has a great deal hung on it is weighed down, heavily loaded or burdened.

clue.text: Game in which draw by one point was scripted by Bennett

definitions.note: the clue describes the answer; the answer is a place name

indicators.note: in which says the following pieces sit inside the game's name

blocks.note: fives is a handball game played in a court
to tow is to draw along
N, north, is one point of the compass

explanation.surface: A sporting match ending level by a single point was written up by a playwright named Bennett.
explanation.walkthrough: Arnold Bennett set his novels in the Five Towns, his fictional version of the Staffordshire Potteries; 'Game' is the handball game, not a match.
explanation.definitionFit: The Potteries towns of Staffordshire were fictionalised by novelist Arnold Bennett under that collective name in Anna of the Five Towns.

clue.text: Assigned task of putting clock back

indicators.note: putting a clock back sends it the other way, so the word for clock is read from its end

blocks.note: a timer is a clock

explanation.surface: Someone is given the job of turning the clocks back an hour.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests the autumn change of the clocks; 'putting ... back' turns TIMER round.
explanation.definitionFit: A remit is the area of responsibility or brief formally given to someone, the job they have been handed.

clue.text: Numbers need editor: the crossword setter's taken the plunge

blocks.note: nos is the abbreviation for numbers
ed is the abbreviation for editor
the setter's is I have, contracted to I've

explanation.surface: A crossword setter decides to risk it after being told the numbers need an editor.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter refers to himself, so 'the crossword setter's' is I've, written IVE in the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: A steep headlong dive, especially of an aircraft, is a sudden plunge downwards.

clue.text: Favourite soldier getting about an awful lot may be full of spirit

indicators.note: awful suggests something badly done, so the letters of the word after it are jumbled
getting about means going round, so the soldier surrounds the jumbled letters

blocks.note: a pet is a favourite
a ranker is a soldier in the ranks
taken as written

explanation.surface: A beloved soldier who drinks a great deal may well be full of the spirit.
explanation.walkthrough: The jumbled letters go in after the soldier's first letter. Spirit here is motor spirit, the British name for petrol.
explanation.definitionFit: A road vehicle carrying fuel in bulk is loaded with motor spirit, which is another name for petrol.

clue.text: Propagated by philosopher who's been conducted outside

indicators.note: outside says the word for conducted wraps round the philosopher

blocks.note: A J Ayer was a British philosopher
led means conducted

explanation.surface: A thinker's ideas were spread by being escorted around.
explanation.walkthrough: In gardening, layering propagates a plant by pegging a stem into soil until it roots, so the definition is not about spreading ideas.
explanation.definitionFit: Gardeners propagate plants by layering, bending a stem down to root in the soil while still attached to its parent.

clue.text: Catcher where there's a rift that's crescent-shaped

indicators.note: where locates the catcher inside the object described next

blocks.note: Tennyson wrote of the little rift within the lute
a net catches things

explanation.surface: A catch is made at a point where a crescent-shaped crack has opened.
explanation.walkthrough: Tennyson's line 'the little rift within the lute' is the source of the phrase; the instrument is what has the rift.
explanation.definitionFit: A lunette is a half-moon shaped object or space, such as an arched window or a fortification shaped like a crescent.

clue.text: Prince and queen, perhaps, in board game

blocks.note: Prince Hal is Shakespeare's young Henry V
a queen is a mother cat, and ma is a mother

explanation.surface: A prince and a queen appear as pieces in a game of chess or similar.
explanation.walkthrough: A queen is a breeding female cat, so a mother; 'perhaps' flags the example. Chess has a queen, but the game here is a different one.
explanation.definitionFit: Halma is a Victorian strategy game played by moving pieces across a squared playing surface, a forerunner of Chinese chequers.

clue.text: The boys in green are not responsible

blocks.note: first meaning: the folk song Green Grow the Rushes, O has 'two, two, the ... boys, clothed all in green'
second meaning: innocent, free of any blame

explanation.surface: Some young men dressed in green insist they are blameless.
explanation.walkthrough: The first half quotes the old counting song Green Grow the Rushes, O, where the second verse names the lily-white boys dressed all in green.
explanation.definitionFit: Lily-white means spotlessly pure, so figuratively innocent and blameless, carrying no guilt for what happened.

clue.text: Craft on the hawthorn

blocks.note: first meaning: the ship that carried the Pilgrim Fathers to America in 1620
second meaning: the blossom of the hawthorn, which is called may

explanation.walkthrough: Hawthorn is also called may, so its blossom is a may flower; the famous ship took the Pilgrims across the Atlantic.
explanation.definitionFit: The Pilgrim Fathers' ship shares its name with the hawthorn's white spring blossom, known in Britain as may.

clue.text: Endure Jack injuring camel

blocks.note: to last is to endure
Jack Straw was a British Labour cabinet minister

explanation.surface: A man called Jack keeps on hurting a camel.
explanation.walkthrough: Jack Straw was Home Secretary when this puzzle appeared. The proverbial final straw is the one that breaks the camel's back.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb says it is the final small load that breaks the camel's back, so it is what injures the beast.

clue.text: Powell's little house built in Powys

definitions.note: the clue gives a location; the answer is a town there

indicators.note: something built is put together from parts, so these letters are assembled anew

blocks.note: taken as written
ho is the abbreviation for house

explanation.surface: A Welshman named Powell has had a small home put up in his county.
explanation.walkthrough: Powys is a county in mid Wales; Welshpool is a market town in it.
explanation.definitionFit: Welshpool is a market town near the English border, located within the Welsh county of Powys.

clue.text: Figure of a man in charge with label attached

blocks.note: OC is the officer commanding a unit
a tag is a label
on can mean attached, as with a lid that is on

explanation.surface: The boss is pictured wearing a name badge.
explanation.walkthrough: OC, Officer Commanding, is the military abbreviation for the person in charge of a unit.
explanation.definitionFit: An eight-sided polygon is a geometric figure, so the word names a shape in the mathematical sense.

clue.text: Little girl on strike because she canêt have the job?

definitions.text: because she canêt have the job?

indicators.note: in a down clue, on means placed underneath, so the girl's name comes below the word for strike

blocks.note: to lam is to beat or strike
Beth is a short form of Elizabeth

explanation.surface: A young girl walks out in protest at being refused a job.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'on' puts the girl underneath. Lambeth Palace is the London seat of the Archbishop of Canterbury, a post then closed to women.
explanation.definitionFit: Lambeth stands for the Church of England's leadership, which at the time barred women from becoming bishops.

clue.text: Rope-maker of Paris is a Londoner

indicators.note: of says the answer is made out of the words that follow, taken from inside them

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of Paris, all of is, a, and the start of Londoner

explanation.surface: A rope manufacturer from France turns out to be a Londoner.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface invites thinking of Paris the city or French words; the letters simply run across the words.
explanation.definitionFit: Sisal is a stiff plant fibre from an agave, widely twisted into twine and cordage.

clue.text: Wild boar with two craft

indicators.note: wild means out of control, so the letters run riot into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A wild pig sits in a pair of boats.
explanation.definitionFit: A small boat propelled by oars is a vessel, and craft is a general word for boats.

clue.text: Too drunk to squeak?

blocks.note: surface reading: someone so intoxicated they cannot make a sound
setter's reading: a hinge treated with lubricant no longer squeaks, and the same word is slang for tipsy

explanation.walkthrough: The word is slang for drunk, and also describes a lubricated hinge that has stopped squeaking.
explanation.definitionFit: Well lubricated machinery runs silently, and the same participle is British slang for being intoxicated.

clue.text: Lashes await when master fell upon painter

definitions.note: the clue describes what the answer is for; the answer is a noun

indicators.note: to fall upon is to seize or engulf, so the master's letters close round the next piece

blocks.note: an MC is a master of ceremonies
as can mean when
an ARA is an Associate of the Royal Academy

explanation.surface: A cruel master attacked an artist, who now awaits a whipping.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface lashes are a flogging, but the definition means eyelashes and what is applied to them.
explanation.definitionFit: Mascara is cosmetic colouring brushed onto eyelashes, so it is what the lashes wait to receive.

clue.text: Boundary? Then I'll be shy, be shy

blocks.clueFragment: Then I'll be shy, be shy
blocks.note: surface reading: someone declaring they will be timid
setter's reading: write the IOUs of someone short of money after the word and it becomes a word for aiming high, a shy being a throw

explanation.walkthrough: Shy means short of money, when one writes IOUs; adding IOUS to the answer gives AMBITIOUS, and a shy is also a throw or attempt.
explanation.definitionFit: An ambit is the bounds or scope of something, the limits within which it extends.

clue.text: Face villain that doesn't start conversation

indicators.note: not starting means losing the opening, so the first letter of the word goes

blocks.note: dial is slang for face
a rogue is a villain

explanation.surface: A confrontation with a scoundrel who will not get going.
explanation.walkthrough: Dial for face is old British slang.
explanation.definitionFit: A dialogue is a spoken exchange between two or more people, a talk or discussion.

clue.text: Cubic character with kings for tips

indicators.note: for tips says the end letters at each side are swapped out and replaced

blocks.note: taken as written
R, rex, and K are both abbreviations for king

explanation.surface: A boxy figure in a pack of cards has kings at both ends.
explanation.walkthrough: The two C's at the ends of CUBIC become R and K. Erno Rubik invented the famous puzzle cube.
explanation.definitionFit: Erno Rubik, the Hungarian inventor of the colourful twisting puzzle, is the person most associated with cubes.

clue.text: Drowned, perhaps, marryin' the offspring of Spooner?

indicators.note: Spooner was famed for swapping the opening sounds of words, so the phrase is said that way

blocks.note: to wed is to marry and a daughter is offspring; swapping the W and D sounds gives the answer

explanation.surface: A rustic voice asks about marrying into the Spooner family.
explanation.walkthrough: The dropped g of marryin' is there so the phrase reads like the spoken one. 'Perhaps' marks drowned as one example of being dead in the water.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone drowned lies lifeless in a lake or sea, literally; the idiom also means a plan that has failed.
